## Report: Gonthier, "A Computer-Checked Proof of the Four Colour Theorem"

**1. The question, frozen.** The title and opening make central: is there a fully computer-checked proof of the Four Colour Theorem, and how does it work? Underneath sits the substantive explanation: *why do four colours suffice for any simple planar map?* I freeze the second, since it is what the paper's parts do work for. Range: every simple planar map (regions are connected open sets; adjacent only where closures meet away from corners); the proof then restricts to finite bridgeless connected polygonal maps. Kind of question: *why can it not happen* — a block, showing no five-colour counterexample survives. Contrast: why four and not five. The paper also answers a second question, "what makes this proof trustworthy," noted but not tested here.

**2. The explanation in parts** (the owner's words): hypermaps (darts plus three permutations e, n, f with e∘n∘f = Id); the Euler formula #e+#n+#f = #d + 2#(e∪n∪f) taken as the definition of "planar"; the discretization lemma; reduction to plain cubic maps; a minimal five-colour counterexample; a face of five sides or fewer (Euler); the 32 discharge rules reused from Robertson et al.; discharging to show every low-arity second neighbourhood contains one of the 633 configurations R; the reducibility check (Kempe chains, chromograms, MDD fixpoint); the Birkhoff lemma and theorem (internally 5-connected, spoke rings); the "quiz" embedding; the Coq kernel with computational reflection; the tactic shell; the real-number model.

**3. Part by part** — one mark each, never totalled.

| Part | Mark |
|---|---|
| Hypermap representation (three permutations) | Held — by the job of making planarity computable; the theorem is about maps, so this is the chosen stand-in |
| Euler formula as definition of planar | Held — proved equivalent to the contour Jordan property |
| Discretization lemma | Held — carries continuous maps to combinatorial ones |
| Reduction to cubic/plain | Held — dropping it leaves the counting and enumeration unworkable |
| 32 discharge rules | Fitted — imported and tuned by Robertson et al. on their cases |
| The 633-configuration list R | Loose — Appel–Haken's different list also worked; the held thing is *some finite R* doing both jobs |
| Reducibility computation | Held — does the reducibility job; the MDD/complement machinery is Loose (a simpler store would do, only slower) |
| Birkhoff lemma and theorem | Held — supplies the ring shapes unavoidability needs |
| Quiz / embedding | Held — links check success to actual embedding |
| Coq kernel + reflection | Borrowed — rests on Coq's metatheory, checked here for the script but not for itself |
| Tactic shell | Idle for the theorem's truth (removing it changes script length, not correctness); Held only for the formalization job |
| Real model | Borrowed — the C-Corn/Dedekind construction pins the axioms' consistency |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
*Flip:* had the opposite held, the same parts could not have covered it — the counting pushes arities below six, a fact specific to four colours. Passes.
*Direction:* forward, from causes (Euler → discharging → reducibility). Not a backwards fit.
*Hunt the answer in the starting points:* the conclusion is not sitting in a label — "reducible" is *computed* from edge colourings, not assumed. But two parts (R and the discharge rules) were tuned until they worked together, so those carry fitted content.
*Jobs and provenance:* the theorem's jobs (all maps, all colourings) are given by the statement; the formalization's jobs were set by the author. Marked separately.
*Pull:* a real tension — a larger list R or larger ring size makes unavoidability easier but reducibility harder; Appel–Haken adjusted rules to shrink R, Robertson et al. found the simpler rules. The line is drawn by compute budget and is worth checking.
*Catch-alls:* none. R is finite and explicit; the range limits (bridgeless, connected) are named up front with a discretization lemma, not slipped in after failure.
*Change list, covered:* drop the five-colour assumption; enlarge rings; swap R; weaken planarity. *Left out, openly:* non-simple (multi-piece) maps, the Empire problem — stated, with its count corrected.
*Where parts came from:* the hypermaps, Birkhoff results and the reducibility algorithms were **built**; the configuration catalog and discharge rules were **fitted** (reused, tested only on the cases that produced them); the logic and reals are **borrowed**.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.**
Two moves. (a) Derive the discharge rules rather than import them — that turns the fitted part into a built one and exposes it to cases it has never met. (b) Put a gauge on `check_reducible`: feed a deliberately wrong list and confirm the check rejects it, so we know it is not simply agreeing with whatever it is given.

**6. What this does not show.** Hard-to-vary is not the same as true. A checked script does not certify four colours beyond what Coq's logic encodes, and the proof bottoms out in borrowed parts — the kernel, the compiler, the hardware — which the author names plainly. "Fully checked" narrows the manual-verification job; it does not eliminate trust, it moves it to parts used everywhere and tested on other work.

**7. One next step.** Write a short pre-registered prediction: which part of the reals/topology stack the discretization lemma should *fail* on if planarity were dropped, then run it — to see whether that link is doing the work claimed, or only reporting it.
